A 2% insurance deductible needs a base: turn the percentage into the household’s cash share

Compare a hypothetical insured-value percentage with a loss-based percentage and a flat amount, then chart the accepted loss share and reserve gap.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Translate an insured-value percentage deductible into a household loss share and reserve gap

Interactive planning lab

Deductible threshold: percentage × declared insured basis$12,000
Household share of the selected accepted damage$12,000
Additional cash for that share after the assigned reserve$4,000

Original hypothetical single-loss settlement in CAD, not a policy quote, claim decision, Canadian insurance rule or implementation of a U.S. storm policy. This teaching contract applies one percentage to the entered declared insured-value basis. For damage already accepted as covered, household share = min(damage, percentage × insured basis), and insurer share = max(0, damage − that threshold). Supported damage never exceeds the minimum declared basis; the example adds no policy-limit shortfall. The loss-based percentage and flat-dollar rows are different assumed rules for comparison, not alternative deductibles the claimant may choose. The cash reserve funds only the final household share; it does not model paying the whole repair invoice before reimbursement. No peril trigger, minimum deductible, aggregate, repeated claim, sublimit, coinsurance, exclusion, depreciation, premium difference, tax, claim probability or payment lag is included. The declared basis is an input, not a market value, purchase price or recommended insurance amount. A threshold above the accepted damage does not make the household owe more than that damage under this stated formula.

The central idea

Read what the percentage multiplies. A deductible based on declared insured value can be much larger than the same percentage of a repair bill, and it can change when that declared base changes.

01

The percentage alone does not identify the cash amount

A percentage deductible is incomplete without its base. Two descriptions can both contain “2%” and still assign very different amounts of an accepted loss to the household.

The U.S. National Association of Insurance Commissioners’ hurricane-deductible explainer describes percentage deductibles that use a home’s insured value. It also explains that the applicable triggers depend on the contract and jurisdiction. That source supplies a concrete reason to inspect the base; it does not establish a Canadian rule or determine which deductible applies to a particular loss.

This article uses an original teaching contract stated in CAD. Its declared insured-value basis is CAD 600,000 and its deductible is 2% of that basis. A single CAD 40,000 damage amount has already been accepted as covered. The charts assume the rule applies and focus on the arithmetic after that assumption.

The tool does not decide coverage, value a building or reproduce a real storm policy. All permitted damage inputs are no greater than the minimum declared basis, so a separate policy-limit shortfall does not enter this particular calculation.

02

Calculate the threshold before comparing it with the damage

The deductible threshold in the teaching contract is CAD 600,000 × 2% = CAD 12,000. It is not CAD 40,000 × 2%. Under the stated single-loss formula, the household bears the smaller of the accepted damage and that threshold.

For the selected CAD 40,000 damage, the household share is therefore CAD 12,000 and the insurer share is CAD 28,000. The two amounts add to the same CAD 40,000 accepted loss.

Although the contract label contains 2%, the household’s share is 12,000 ÷ 40,000, or 30% of this selected loss. The 2% and 30% describe different relationships: the threshold as a share of insured value, and the household portion as a share of damage. Neither percentage can replace the other.

The insured-value basis is an entered contract amount. The tool does not equate it with a property’s sale price, mortgage balance, original purchase price or a recommended reconstruction estimate.

03

Use alternative formulas to expose the difference in bases

The first chart compares three separate teaching rules for the same CAD 40,000 damage. The entered insured-value rule assigns CAD 12,000 to the household. A different rule charging 2% of the damage would assign CAD 800. A separate CAD 2,000 flat-dollar threshold would assign CAD 2,000.

The corresponding insurer portions are CAD 28,000, CAD 39,200 and CAD 38,000. Each stacked bar totals the same accepted damage. What changes is the division of that loss, not the amount of damage.

These countercases are not three options a claimant can select after an event. Nor are they quotes with identical premiums, coverage and eligibility. Their purpose is to show why the written basis must be understood before using the percentage in a cash plan.

Actual contracts may have minimum amounts, different triggers, per-occurrence rules, annual aggregates or other adjustments. None is inferred from the three rows, and no premium comparison or policy recommendation follows from them.

04

A threshold is not an extra bill when the loss is smaller

Change the accepted damage to CAD 5,000 while leaving the CAD 12,000 threshold unchanged. In this formula, the household bears CAD 5,000 and the insurer portion is zero. The calculation does not make the household pay CAD 12,000 on top of that repair.

The loss curve therefore rises with damage until it reaches CAD 12,000, then levels off at that threshold within the simplified covered-loss range. At zero damage both portions are zero. With a zero deductible percentage, the household share is zero throughout this assumed covered-loss formula.

The curve also includes the loss-based countercase, whose household share grows at 2% of damage instead. That line answers a different contract question. The contrast makes the difference in bases visible over a range of losses, not only at one example amount.

The plateau does not promise that a real policy caps every household cost at the deductible. Exclusions, sublimits, uninsured amounts, depreciation and other claim adjustments can change the result. This tool deliberately models none of them.

05

Fund the household portion, and keep reimbursement timing as a separate question

The default assigned cash reserve is CAD 8,000. Against the selected CAD 12,000 household portion, the additional funding requirement is CAD 4,000. The reserve bridge shows CAD 12,000 less CAD 8,000, rather than subtracting the reserve from the entire CAD 40,000 loss and calling that a deductible gap.

If assigned cash exceeds the household portion, the model uses only the amount needed and leaves the rest available. Its additional funding gap is floored at zero. With CAD 5,000 of damage and the original CAD 8,000 reserve, there is no extra final-share funding gap and CAD 3,000 of assigned cash remains unused.

This is a final loss-sharing calculation, not a settlement calendar. A contractor’s invoice may come before an insurer’s payment. Funding that temporary timing difference needs a separate cash bridge, even when the eventual household portion is fully covered by an existing reserve.

The related reimbursement guide examines that timing issue. The related fixed-deductible guide considers premium and reserve trade-offs, while the rebuilding guide addresses coverage limits. Those are distinct from identifying the base of this percentage.

06

An unchanged percentage can still produce a different dollar threshold

Increase the declared basis from CAD 600,000 to CAD 800,000, holding the 2% rate and CAD 40,000 accepted damage fixed. The threshold rises from CAD 12,000 to CAD 16,000. With the same CAD 8,000 assigned reserve, the additional funding requirement rises from CAD 4,000 to CAD 8,000.

The matrix varies the percentage and declared basis while retaining the selected damage and reserve. Larger thresholds increase the household portion only until that portion reaches the accepted damage amount. At that point, an even larger threshold does not create more damage under the stated formula.

The grid contains alternative arithmetic cases without probability weights. It does not suggest lowering a building’s insurance amount to reduce a deductible. Choosing an appropriate insured value and checking the full coverage terms requires a different assessment.

07

Record the complete rule beside the amount reserved

A useful planning record includes the applicable event, the base the percentage multiplies, the percentage itself, any dollar minimum or other adjustment, and whether the rule applies per event or on another basis. Then translate the supported rule into a dollar amount before comparing it with available cash.

The NAIC page reviewed for this article was last updated on 2 June 2025. Its U.S. context is used only to explain why insured-value percentage deductibles need careful reading. The article applies no state trigger, statutory threshold or Canadian policy condition.

The chart inputs are transparent assumptions. For an actual household, the policy wording and confirmed claim treatment control the calculation. The practical lesson is to preserve the denominator and the settlement assumptions, rather than placing an unexplained percentage in the budget.
